_comment: Editor v2 Phase 8 — FROZEN numeric policy authority (Gate-0 §4/§7). Every number the compiler uses lives here and nowhere else. Values marked (gate0) are frozen by docs/editor-v2-phase8-gate0.md §4 and may not be changed without a new Gate-0 decision; the rest were chosen at Batch 8.1 and are frozen from this point. ALL quantities are integers: times in milliseconds, gains in milli-dB, scales in milli-units (1060 == 1.060x). Floating point never enters the plan, so canonical bytes are identical across processes and architectures.
_pacingComment: WHAT calm/balanced/punchy MEAN, IN NUMBERS.
The Director has always decided `pacing`. Until now the compiler read the
field and threw it away, so the model was spending tokens on a choice with
no effect on any video. This block is that choice given meaning.
PACING CONTROLS ONE THING: HOW MUCH SILENCE SURVIVES. It deliberately does
not touch caption style (the Director already picks captionPresetId
separately, and caption-punchy-word-v1 exists), zooms, or transitions.
Bundling those would make four independent decisions impossible to reason
about one at a time, and would couple choices that are currently working.
A PROFILE LISTS ONLY WHAT IT CHANGES. Anything it omits keeps the frozen
`cuts` value above. That is why `balanced` is EMPTY: it is not a set of
numbers that happen to match today, it is the absence of any override, so
it cannot drift out of agreement with `cuts` and cannot overwrite a value
a caller deliberately set.
The first draft of this block got that wrong -- it spelled `balanced` out
as three absolute numbers equal to the `cuts` values. That looks identical
and is not: it silently REPLACED whatever a caller had set, so a test (or
any future code) that lowered maxCutsPerMinuteMilli had its value quietly
restored to 30000 by the default pacing. Deltas remove the failure mode
rather than documenting it.
This is the safety property of the whole change: wiring pacing cannot alter
a single video that already renders correctly, because the default path
returns the identical policy object untouched. Only a recording the
Director actually marked calm or punchy comes out different, so if these
numbers are wrong the blast radius is two modes, not all three.
Note punchy omits minRemovalMs entirely -- it does not differ from the
frozen floor, and repeating the value would be a second place to drift.
WHY PUNCHY DOES NOT CUT SHORTER GAPS. The obvious version of punchy lowers
minRemovalMs toward zero. It must not: minPhonemeHandleMs is 60, so every
cut already needs 60 ms of audio handle on each side, and a 120 ms removal
is the smallest thing that is an edit rather than a glitch. Below that a
cut lands inside natural word spacing and clips speech -- which does not
sound fast, it sounds broken. Punchy therefore buys its speed from the
DENSITY CEILING (45 cuts/min vs 30), not from cutting closer to the words.
WHY CALM RAISES BOTH THE FLOOR AND THE PAUSE GUARD. Raising minRemovalMs to
400 ms means only real dead air is removed and the rhythm between phrases
survives. The density ceiling then does the rest for free: when the cap is
exceeded the compiler keeps the LONGEST removals and gives back the
shortest (see 'cut density' in editorCompile.ts), so a low ceiling
automatically means only the biggest silences get cut. The pause guard goes
UP because a deliberate beat before a key word is the main tool a calm
delivery has; trimming those turns calm into merely slow.
THESE NUMBERS ARE CHOSEN, NOT MEASURED, and that is recorded here rather
than hidden. They are set against how short-form content actually cuts
(one cut every 5s / 2s / 1.3s), which is reasoning, not evidence -- the same
kind of reasoning that produced a 50-minute CI cap when the real figure was
77, a 25% hook-trim threshold that refused a legitimate 28.7% case, and an
80 ms caption tail guard against a real 93-120 ms shortfall.
So this ships the way loudness did: enforce the band, and RECORD the real
distribution. compileEditPlan returns cut-density stats on every render, so
these three columns get corrected from what actually happens to real
videos instead of remaining an estimate with no expiry date.
_edgesComment: THE EDGES OF A RECORDING ARE ALWAYS WASTE, and until now removing them was
left to the Director's discretion. It is not a judgement call. Nobody has
ever wanted their video to open on themselves settling into frame, and
nobody has ever wanted it to end on themselves reaching for the stop
button -- which the creator is ALWAYS doing, because they are the one
The hook mechanism already trims the head when the Director chooses to open
on a word. This is the floor beneath that: with or without a hook, whatever
sits outside the first and last spoken word is removed.
keepMs leaves a small breath so the first word does not start on frame one
and the last does not end abruptly. minTrimMs stops a 40ms sliver being
recorded as an edit -- the same reasoning as cuts.minRemovalMs.
_hookComment: HOW MUCH OF A RECORDING A HOOK CHOICE MAY DISCARD.
hookTreatment 'open_at_word' drops everything before a chosen word, and
the only guard was 'did it remove ALL the media'. So a Director picking a
late word could silently discard most of a take: a 60s recording becomes
a 6s video, the plan validates, the render succeeds, and nothing anywhere
says why. The creator sees a video missing the middle of what they said.
A hook trim exists to drop a greeting or preamble -- 'hey guys, welcome
back, so today' -- which is seconds, not tens of seconds. Both bounds
must hold: 15s absolute, and half the accepted material.
The fraction was first set at a quarter and that was a GUESS -- it refused
an existing, legitimate case (a 12.9s open-at-word over a 45s domain,
28.7%, which the suite already asserted works). Refusing real behaviour on
an unmeasured threshold is the mistake roomyEarlyEnergyRatioMilliMax made.
Half is where 'discarded most of the recording' actually begins, and the
15s absolute carries the rest: a greeting is seconds, so any trim long
enough to matter trips the absolute long before the fraction.
Exceeding either does NOT fail the render. It falls back to keeping the
real opening and says so, mirroring hook_open_at_word_noop, which already
establishes that an unusable hook choice is announced and not applied.
_titleHookComment: THE VISUAL HOOK — three to five big words on screen at the very start.
Why this exists at all: a creator with a million followers, whose whole
business is short-form, puts it plainly -- a VISUAL hook is worth far more
than a spoken one, because people read faster than they listen. Until now
TwinAI burned subtitles of what is BEING SAID and never put a title on
screen. The edit plan had no element for one.
WHERE THE WORDS COME FROM, and why not from the model. The text is the
creator's OWN FIRST SPOKEN WORDS, taken from the caption cues that already
survived the cut. That makes it impossible to fabricate a claim, impossible
to misspell a brand name the ASR never heard correctly, and impossible for
an injected instruction to reach the screen -- the same anti-fabrication
rule the rest of this path runs on, where nothing is invented and
everything references pinned evidence. Letting the Director choose better
words is a real improvement and a SEPARATE change, because it adds a
decision the model can get wrong and a contract both copies must agree on.
durationMs 2000: the same source puts the short-form attention window at
about four seconds, so a title that outlives half of it is competing with
the content it was meant to sell. Two seconds is long enough to read five
words and short enough to get out of the way.
marginTopPx 420 IS PROVISIONAL AND SAYS SO. It clears the platform tab bar
at the top of the feed and sits above where a face usually is in a vertical
talking-head frame. That is reasoning, not measurement -- exactly what the
safe-zone ruler exists to replace. It is recorded here as the next value to
correct once a real screenshot lands, rather than quietly frozen as if it
were measured.
minWords 2 is a REFUSAL threshold, not a target: a one-word title is not a
hook, it is a fragment, and showing it would look like a bug. When fewer
than two words survive, there is simply no title.

_tailGuardComment: How far before the END OF THE PLANNED DURATION the last caption must finish.
The output validator compares cues to the MEASURED duration with ZERO
tolerance, because a cue past the end means the caption and video
timelines came from different maps. Crucially it measures the VIDEO
STREAM, not the container: the container reports the longer of the two
streams, while the video stream truncates to whole frames and to segment
boundaries. Measured on real renders, the video stream lands 93-120 ms
SHORT of the planned duration -- so a guard smaller than that still lets
a caption fall outside the video.
250 ms is not a fresh guess: it is the frozen durationToleranceMs the
output profile already permits the render to differ from the plan by. If
the video may legitimately come in that much shorter, a caption promised
inside that window was never safe. Restated here rather than imported
because Gate-0 s7 forbids the compiler reading the render catalog.
Invisible in practice: the caption leaves a quarter-second before the
video ends, and the words it shows finished before that.
_marginHorizontalComment: How far a caption line stops short of the LEFT and RIGHT edges.
Was 40, hardcoded in assCaptions.ts. MEASURED from a real TikTok feed
screenshot: the like/comment/share rail sits about 100 px in from the
right edge, so a wide centred line at a 40 px margin runs UNDER the
buttons. 140 clears the rail with room, and because the style is centred
it costs a little width on both sides rather than shifting the text
marginVerticalPx went 320/360 -> 600 in the same change, and that one is
the bigger fix: Instagram stacks a comment bar, a likes row, a username
row and the caption itself, reaching ~500-650 px up in frame
coordinates. Captions at 320 were underneath all of it. 600 is chosen
high on purpose -- slightly too high still looks fine, hidden ruins the
video -- and is provisional until the safe-zone ruler gives the exact
_maxWidthComment: THE COLLISION IS THE ACTION RAIL, AND IT IS HORIZONTAL.
MEASURED, at last, from a safe-zone ruler the creator posted and
screenshotted in both feeds -- the measurement this file has been waiting
for since marginVerticalPx was raised to 600 'provisional until the
safe-zone ruler gives the exact number'.
TikTok (17 Pro Max)    rail ~200 px in from the right edge
Reels  (11 Pro Max)    rail ~150-200 px in from the right edge
icons in the 320-360 band: TikTok bookmark ~340, Reels share ~370 /
send ~320
THE BOTTOM CAPTION BLOCK WAS NEVER THE PROBLEM. TikTok's caption/username
block sits ~130-200 px up and Reels' ~60-110 px, both far below the 600 px
captions already clear. Raising the band further does not help and cannot:
the rail runs UP the side of the frame, so escaping it vertically means
clearing the heart at ~600 px, which would put captions in the middle of
the video. marginVerticalPx is therefore UNCHANGED at 600 -- the fix is
width, not height.
WHY A MAX WIDTH RATHER THAN JUST A BIGGER MARGIN. The two are the same
number today (1080 - 2*200 == 680), but they are not the same CLAIM. The
margin is a knob someone may reasonably retune for typography; the width
is the thing the rail actually constrains. Recording both lets the
contract test assert the relationship between them, so lowering the margin
for a nicer line length fails CI instead of quietly sliding a caption back
under the bookmark button.
railInsetPx is the measurement itself, kept separate from the width so the
arithmetic stays visible: any centred line wider than
playResX - 2*railInsetPx has a corner under the rail, because centring
spends every extra pixel on BOTH sides.
maxCharsPerLine IS STILL A CHARACTER PROXY (see fragmentToken in
editorCompile.ts -- 'the renderer measures nothing here'). It is now a
proxy that has been MEASURED against the pinned font rather than chosen:
caption-line-width.test.ts reads DejaVuSans-Bold's own advance widths and
reports the pixel width each preset's ceiling actually produces.
THE FIRST MEASUREMENT SAID THE PRESETS DID NOT FIT, BY A LOT. At 22/16/32
characters, ordinary English caption text drew 1.45x-1.57x the 680px box.
The note that used to sit here said libass would re-wrap such a line
inside the box, making it a planned-vs-rendered line-count mismatch rather
than a safe-area breach. THAT WAS WRONG, and it is the reason the gap read
as tolerable for as long as it did: assCaptions emits WrapStyle 2, which
is 'no word wrapping'. libass breaks only on the compiler's own \N, so an
over-wide line is not re-wrapped at all -- it is drawn wider than the box,
straight through the rail inset railInsetPx exists to keep clear.
The ceilings below are the measured fit: 13/10/17. caption-minimal-
subtitle-v1 also drops from 8 words per cue to 5, because 8 words cannot
fit two lines of a 680px box at ANY character count that does not
fragment ordinary words -- that preset's real constraint was its word
budget, not its font size. Lowering a ceiling costs cue COUNT and never
text: compileEditPlan gives an overflowing tail back to the next cue
rather than dropping it.
WHAT THIS STILL DOES NOT CLAIM. A proxy measured against a corpus is not
a per-line measurement. A line of capital Ws at 13 characters is still
wider than the box; what is claimed is that ordinary caption text at
these ceilings fits, which is what the pinned measurement checks.
_scriptSpellingComment: CAPTIONS TAKE THE SCRIPT'S SPELLING AT THE RECORDING'S TIME.
The script is ground truth for SPELLING; the recording is ground truth for
TIMING. Until now captions used the ASR's spelling for both, so a brand
name, a handle or any jargon the ASR never heard correctly went on screen
misspelled even though the creator had typed it correctly minutes earlier.
APPLIED ONLY TO SUBSTITUTIONS. The aligner classifies every script word as
match / substitution / not-spoken, plus insertions for ad-libs. Only a
SUBSTITUTION is re-spelled -- the aligner put a script word and a spoken
word in the same position and they differ. A `match` needs nothing. A
`not_spoken` word was never said and must never appear. An INSERTION is an
ad-lib and keeps the ASR's text, because editorSpeech requires off-script
words to survive: the transcript is evidence, and evidence is not edited
to agree with the plan.
So this can only ever CHANGE THE SPELLING OF A WORD THE ALIGNER ALREADY
PAIRED. It cannot add, drop, reorder or retime a caption word. That bound
is the reason this is safe to apply to every render rather than gated.
WHY A SIMILARITY FLOOR. A substitution with high similarity is the ASR
mishearing something close -- 'twinny' for 'TwinAI' -- and the script is
right. A substitution with LOW similarity is more likely the creator
genuinely saying something else, where the aligner has paired two unrelated
words simply because they occupy the same position. Re-spelling that one
would put a word on screen the creator never said, which is the one failure
this must not have. The floor buys that safety at the cost of leaving some
legitimate corrections unmade -- the right direction to err.
700/1000 IS CHOSEN, NOT MEASURED, and that is recorded here rather than
hidden -- the same discipline the pacing block and the hook trim fraction
are held to, both of which record that a guessed threshold has already
refused legitimate cases on this project. compileEditPlan therefore returns
a count of how many words were re-spelled and how many were refused by the
floor, so this number gets corrected from what actually happens to real
videos instead of remaining an estimate with no expiry date.
_scriptSpellingEnabledComment: THE OFF SWITCH. Set false and captions revert to the ASR's spelling
everywhere, exactly as they read before this feature existed -- no code
change, no logic change, one boolean.
It exists because the failure mode here is a WRONG WORD ON SCREEN in a
video somebody has already posted, and the remedy must not be 'wait for a
patch'. Lowering the floor is the precise fix once you know which word
went wrong; this is the blunt one you can reach for first and think
afterwards. Reverting is always available and always total.
The floor and the switch are separate on purpose: a floor of 1000 would
very nearly disable the feature but not quite, and 'nearly off' is not a
state anyone wants to reason about while looking at a bad video.
_glossaryComment: THE GLOSSARY FLOOR — the floor a substitution clears when the SCRIPT word
is a term the creator typed into their permanent glossary (§6, 'any hard
The ordinary floor exists because a substitution is the ALIGNER'S GUESS
that two words are the same word. A glossary term is evidence that
reduces that risk for exactly one word: the creator typed it,
deliberately, as a word they expect to be got wrong.
400 is CHOSEN, not measured — the same honest state the 700 above is in,
and the reason `glossaryAdmitted` rides out on every render. That number
counts the re-spellings admitted ONLY because of the glossary, so it is
both the evidence the feature works and the evidence it went too far.
Correct it from real videos, not from this comment.
It must be BELOW the ordinary floor to do anything: a higher value would
remove re-spellings for exactly the words the creator flagged as
important, so the compiler treats a higher one as 'no glossary' rather
